description: 🌱🛰️ Ceres Agronauts es un equipo dedicado a explorar cómo la ciencia y la tecnología espacial pueden transformar el sector agropecuario. Buscamos desarrollar soluciones innovadoras y sostenibles para mejorar la producción agrícola, optimizar los recursos naturales y contribuir al futuro del campo.
summary:
We developed an agronomic decision-support tool built for both farmers and agronomists in San Luis, Argentina, designed for that critical moment at the start of a season when the core question arises: “What should I plant, what local conditions and challenges does my land face, and which crop rotation works best?”.

The platform is built for everyone, whether they have a background in numbers and data or not. Users enter whatever field information they know; whenever data is missing, the system uses satellite estimates to fill in the environmental parameters. It then runs a calculation combining those inputs with verified local research on San Luis’s climate, soil, water, and pests, adapting its recommendation to the user’s specific priorities—whether producing forage, seeking quick economic returns from an immediate harvest, or building resilience against water scarcity.

Rather than claiming to be an indisputable truth, our tool acts as a reliable, accessible decision-making guide grounded in real scientific sources and satellite observation, helping farmers protect their soil and prevent crop losses.
details:
AGROSPIN 

Better farming decisions start with better evidence.

An agricultural decision-support project for crop rotation, water stress and climate variability.

A local question. Real Earth data. A practical agricultural purpose.

Built around the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: “Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data.”

PILOT AREA  Villa Mercedes, San Luis – southern Córdoba, Argentina

01. THE PROBLEM BEHIND THE PROJECT

Why we started AgroSpin

Farming involves much more than choosing what to plant next. A decision that seems simple on paper can depend on the rainfall of the last few seasons, how much water the soil can store, the risk of a late frost, the demands of each crop, and what the producer can afford to risk.

For small and medium-sized farmers, this information may be scattered across different websites, spreadsheets, field records and technical reports. The challenge is not only to obtain data; it is to understand what the data means for a real farming decision.

That is the idea behind AgroSpin. We want to put relevant environmental and agricultural information in one place and turn it into something useful, clear and easy to discuss before making decisions about crops and rotation.

What does our project do, and how does it work?

AgroSpin brings together historical climate information, local soil characteristics, crop knowledge and farmer priorities. Instead of showing a collection of unrelated numbers, it organizes them into indicators that can help a person understand the conditions of a region or field, and consider different crop rotation strategies.

The idea is to ask practical questions: Has rainfall been reliable? Is the season becoming hotter? How often do frost conditions appear? Is the atmospheric demand for water greater than rainfall? What do we know about the soil, and what are we still missing? Only then do we ask which rotation alternatives are worth evaluating.

For us, the key is that the farmer remains the decision-maker. AgroSpin is meant to provide context, comparisons and reasons, not an unexplained answer or an automatic prescription.

02  WORKING WITH REAL INFORMATION

What we have developed so far

Our pilot is focused on the Villa Mercedes area in San Luis and the neighboring part of southern Córdoba, Argentina. We selected a real geographical area so that the work could move beyond a generic prototype and use concrete environmental data.

As of 15 November 2026, the public repository includes a prepared climate-and-soil data package, with a data cutoff of 1 November 2026. It contains daily, monthly and annual climate series, regional soil layers, ground-station references and crop-related reference data. The information is structured for analytical tools such as Looker Studio and for Python-based processing.

Current project asset

What it contributes

NASA POWER climate series

1991–2026 climate tables for 32 regional grid points, including temperature and precipitation.

Derived agroclimatic indicators

Reference evapotranspiration (ETo), P−ETo, frost and heat-stress days, growing degree days and growing-season context.

Ground weather references

19 terrestrial stations catalogued, including local validation work and documented gaps.

Regional soil context

Topography, slope, soil-profile records, and model-derived moisture with explicit limitations.

Crop knowledge

An eight-crop FAO GAEZ reference layer and a draft crop catalog with FAO-56 parameters.

Exploration and prototype

Prepared Looker Studio datasets; a Python/Streamlit rotation simulation prototype in the codebase.

An important detail is that our data distinguishes observations measured on the ground, modeled or reanalysis estimates, and reference information. This difference matters because a satellite-derived or model-based regional value should never be described as a direct measurement inside a specific farm.

Turning variables into useful indicators

Indicator

Agricultural meaning

Decision it can inform

Rainfall (mm)

How much rain the region received and how it changed over time.

Seasonal water exposure and timing.

ETo and P−ETo

Atmospheric demand for water and a simple climate balance.

Whether crop water needs deserve closer study.

Heat-stress days

Days above a defined temperature threshold.

Potential exposure of sensitive crop stages.

Frost indicators

Cold-event frequency and approximate frost-free windows.

Whether crop calendars may face frost risk.

Soil texture and depth

How soils may differ in storing and supplying water.

Which field data are essential before comparing crops.

Crop Kc and root depth

Crop-related water use and rooting characteristics.

Future crop water-requirement calculations.

A real example from our climate dataset

The chart below compares annual precipitation and reference evapotranspiration (ETo) in the pilot region. It uses the project’s prepared NASA POWER-based annual table, averaged equally across its 32 regional grid points. This is a regional comparison, not a reading taken from an individual field.

When the ETo line is above rainfall, it highlights a potentially important climate pressure. It does not mean that a farm has exactly that amount of water deficit: actual crop stress also depends on stored soil water, runoff, irrigation, crop type, growth stage and local conditions. This distinction is central to our approach.

03 FROM INFORMATION TO ALTERNATIVES

Crop rotation is the decision we want to improve

Crop rotation means changing the crops grown on a field over successive seasons. The purpose is not simply to alternate names on a calendar. Different crop sequences can affect water demand, soil cover, nutrient management, operational timing and the type of financial risk a producer accepts.

Our idea is to compare alternatives instead of assuming that one crop or one sequence is best for everyone. A producer who prioritizes water conservation may look at the same options differently from someone who needs a stable commercial return or wants to improve soil cover. The environmental evidence stays the same; the farmer’s priorities help frame the comparison.

We explored rotations involving crops such as maize, soybean, sorghum, sunflower and alfalfa. The project also considers cover crops and winter-crop possibilities as research topics. We use them to study trade-offs; we do not claim that any sequence is safe, profitable or suitable without local agronomic validation.

What a future comparison should explain: why a rotation may fit the climate, which soil assumptions it relies on, what it could improve, which risks remain, what it might cost in water or management, and which parts of the answer come from solid evidence versus an open hypothesis.

04  /  VALUE FOR PRODUCERS

What benefits does AgroSpin offer?

The first benefit is organization. Farmers and agronomists should not have to interpret disconnected datasets before understanding a basic situation. AgroSpin aims to gather relevant information, standardize it and display it in a way that supports practical discussion.

Clearer decisions about water and climate

Rainfall is important, but it is not the full story. Temperature, extreme heat, evapotranspiration, soil water storage and the timing of a crop all influence the context. By combining these pieces, the project can help reveal questions and risks that might be missed when looking only at annual rainfall.

A longer-term view of the field

The project invites producers to look beyond a single harvest. Rotation choices can influence soil cover, water use and future options. We want the conversation to include resilience and soil condition, not only the immediate result of the next planting season.

Useful information for different users

Our priority is small and medium-sized producers, because advanced data tools are not always accessible to them. At the same time, a clear explanation of the sources and indicators can help agronomists, students, technicians and other farming organizations work with the same evidence.

Transparency instead of blind trust

A meaningful result should show where the information came from, whether it was measured or estimated, the date and scale of the source, and what limitations it has. In agriculture, a number without context can create false confidence. We would rather show a limitation than hide it.

A base we can keep improving

The prepared data tables, documentation, code and validation rules create a reusable foundation. More local observations, farmer feedback and expert review can improve the next version without losing track of what changed.

05  /  THE CHANGE WE HOPE TO MAKE

What impact do we expect?

Our goal is to help small and medium-sized producers make better-informed decisions about how to manage their crops, use their water resources and plan rotations with a clearer view of climate risk. We believe this can support more resilient production and, over time, more careful investment decisions.

There is a very practical business side to this. Every planting decision involves inputs, labor, time and money. If a producer can identify an important risk before committing those resources, or compare the implications of different strategies, that information has value. The long-term ambition is to contribute to more sustainable farm performance and a better return on investment.

We are not claiming a measured financial improvement today. The project has not yet demonstrated a causal increase in yield or profit. Those outcomes would need field trials, operational records and comparison against existing decision processes.

How we would measure impact in a future pilot

Area

A realistic way to measure progress

Accessibility

Can a producer understand the indicators, labels and limitations without special training?

Decision quality

Can a user explain the evidence and trade-offs behind each rotation alternative?

Agronomic relevance

Do local experts judge the rules and assumptions appropriate for the pilot area?

Water and production

Do field measurements or farm records confirm the usefulness of the proposed indicators?

Economic results

Do observed costs, yields and margins improve compared with a meaningful baseline?

We want AgroSpin to be useful beyond a hackathon, but usefulness has to be demonstrated. That is why these impact measures are goals for future validation, not results we have already achieved.

06  /  CREATIVITY AND TEAMWORK

What makes our project creative?

For us, creativity is not only about an attractive interface or a complicated algorithm. It is also about bringing different ways of thinking together to solve one real problem. Our team is multidisciplinary: we contribute experience in data analysis, business processes, software development and engineering-related fields. We do not all look at the same information in the same way, and that has been an advantage.

Some of us are naturally focused on the data: whether it is complete, which variables belong together, and how to explain a metric. Others think about the software, architecture, integrations and how to turn an idea into a working product. The combination creates more questions, more ideas and, importantly, more opportunities to detect mistakes before they become part of the solution.

We also think there is something creative about making complex scientific information understandable. A producer does not need to see every line of code or every satellite file. They need to understand what the situation is, why it matters and what options deserve attention. Turning that complexity into a clear and useful explanation is part of the design.

The other creative decision was to start locally. Instead of trying to cover every crop and every country, we chose a real area in Argentina, collected years of environmental information and worked toward a product that could be tested against local knowledge. That makes the prototype more concrete and gives us a responsible way to grow.

Our creativity comes from the combination: different skills, active participation, a shared agricultural goal, and the willingness to question an idea until it becomes something useful.

07  /  WHAT GUIDED OUR DECISIONS

What factors did our team consider?

We tried to look at the project from the point of view of the people who might actually use it. It would not be enough to build something technically interesting if the producer could not understand it, did not trust it, or could not connect it to a decision.

The producer and the field come first

We considered the needs of small and medium-sized producers, different levels of technical knowledge, and the reality that farms do not all have the same budget, land conditions or priorities. We wanted language that could reach a broad audience without losing the scientific meaning of the information.

Water, climate and soil are connected

We studied precipitation, temperature, heat and frost exposure, reference evapotranspiration, modeled moisture, soil properties and topography. The question was always what each variable could add to the crop-rotation decision, rather than how many sources we could add to a dashboard.

Evidence quality and geographical scale

We considered where the data came from, its time coverage, whether it was observed or estimated, and whether its resolution was appropriate. NASA POWER provides useful regional climate context, but it is not a sensor placed in a farm. Some soil information is local, while other layers remain too coarse or incomplete to justify field-level conclusions.

Agronomic knowledge and uncertainty

We considered crop water requirements, planting windows, rooting depth, the current crop history and possible rotation interactions. Several parameters still require expert review. We intentionally distinguish what is verified, what is being tested and what is only a research idea.

Economic reality and inclusion

We considered that producers must balance environmental risk with costs, labor, equipment, market opportunities and the financial result they need. These economic details are not yet integrated into a validated profit model, but they are essential for a future decision-support product. We also want the tool to be understandable rather than restricted to specialists.

Practical delivery and responsible use of AI

We worked with tools available to the team and our personal computers, prioritizing reproducible and open formats. AI helped us research, organize, write and develop ideas, but it does not replace authoritative datasets or agronomic expertise. The final responsibility for evaluating a result remains with people.

08  /  TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

What tools, languages, software and hardware did we use?

We worked with a combination of familiar tools and technologies that let us move from research to data preparation, visualization and a prototype. Not every tool has the same role: some were used directly, while others form part of the planned architecture.

Category

Tools and contribution

Data and reporting

Google Looker Studio for metrics, filters and exploratory visual reports; CSV and Parquet for analytical datasets.

Languages

Python for data processing and the prototype; HTML and JavaScript for web-oriented work and interface development.

Application and libraries

Python, Pandas and a Streamlit-based exploratory interface; Git and GitHub for versioning and collaboration.

Development software

Linux, Visual Studio Code and Antigravity as part of the team workflow; Paint for quick visual assets.

AI assistance

ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini for brainstorming, explanations, documentation and development support, with human review.

Hardware

Team members’ personal notebooks and available development equipment; no dedicated farm hardware required for the documented data package.

Future / optional architecture

FastAPI and Leaflet are described as integration paths in the MVP data package; they should not be mistaken for a fully deployed, validated platform.


Github repository
https://github.com/Ceres-Astronauts/AgroSpin

The evidence and scientific references behind it

Our data work uses NASA POWER as the principal climate source, with SMAP examined for soil-moisture context. The package also includes relevant regional and scientific references such as SRTM terrain data, NOAA ENSO information, local ground stations, INTA soil profiles and FAO GAEZ crop-suitability layers. The crop catalog documents coefficients and rooting information from FAO-56.

We did not add every possible satellite product just to make the project appear more advanced. ECOSTRESS, HLS, GPM IMERG, GRACE and other sources can be considered when they answer a concrete question that the current evidence cannot answer.

09  /  WHAT WORKS TODAY, AND WHAT COMES NEXT

Where the project stands

Developed and available: a public climate-and-soil MVP data package; prepared tables for analysis and visualization; source documentation and provenance; an initial crop catalog; and Python code for an exploratory Streamlit-based rotation simulator.

Demonstrated / exploratory: Looker Studio charts and filters help visualize climate data. The simulator can illustrate priorities and candidate rotations, but some scenario values and scoring logic are not backed by an end-to-end scientifically validated evaluation.

Still needing validation: parcel-level crop suitability, reliable local soil-water estimates, crop-specific water demand across a complete growing cycle, rotation effects, and any ranking that claims to identify the best crop sequence.

The most important scientific limits

  • The climate grid provides regional context, not precise measurements for a specific farm; resampling does not create additional information.
  • The monthly soil-moisture balance model did not pass the project’s daily-correlation threshold against SMAP; this indicator must be presented with its warning.
  • The terrain-derived topographic susceptibility index is not a validated flood-risk map.
  • Many local soil horizons lack complete texture and field-capacity measurements; the crop catalog and rotation rules also contain unverified parameters.
  • No validated ranking, yield forecast, profit estimate or automatic agronomic prescription should be claimed from the current evidence.

Our next steps

The next meaningful step is not simply to add more charts. It is to connect the prepared environmental data with one field or representative soil case, define a small set of realistic rotations, verify the relevant crop parameters with agronomic sources, and compare alternatives using transparent rules. Then we can test whether farmers and experts actually find the explanations useful.

10  /  OUR CLOSING MESSAGE

A project built around a real need

AgroSpin started with the idea of consolidating agricultural variables and producing useful metrics. As we worked, it became clear that the real value is not the report by itself. It is the possibility of connecting climate, water, soil and crop information to decisions that affect a producer’s work and future.

We want to create something that includes people rather than excluding them with difficult terminology. Something that uses the power of NASA data, but also respects local knowledge, uncertainty and the choices that farmers make every season.

If AgroSpin can help someone ask better questions, understand a risk earlier and compare options more clearly, then it is moving toward the impact we wanted from the beginning.
